tollund-man.name: Tollund Man
tollund-man.summary: A naturally mummified bog body of a man who died by hanging between 405 and 384 BC, found near Silkeborg, Denmark, in 1950 and remarkably well preserved.

nordic-bronze-age.name: Nordic Bronze Age
nordic-bronze-age.summary: A period of Scandinavian prehistory from about 2000/1750 to 500 BC, shaped by Central European metalworking traditions and maintaining trade links with Mycenaean Greece.

celtic-field.name: Celtic field
celtic-field.summary: An old name for traces of prehistoric farming field systems found across North-West Europe, dating from about 1800 BC to the early medieval period, despite not actually being linked to Celtic culture.

lynchet.name: Lynchet
lynchet.summary: An earth terrace on a hillside found in ancient British field systems, likely dug to maximise farmland on slopes; rows of them are called "strip lynchets."

vorbasse.name: Vorbasse
vorbasse.summary: A town in Denmark known for archaeological excavations of a farming settlement occupied from the 1st century BC to the 11th century AD.

o-g-s-crawford.name: O. G. S. Crawford
o-g-s-crawford.summary: British archaeologist (1886–1957) specializing in prehistoric Britain and Sudan, a pioneer of aerial archaeology who worked as archaeological officer for the Ordnance Survey.

gundestrup-cauldron.name: Gundestrup Cauldron
gundestrup-cauldron.summary: A richly decorated silver vessel from around 150 BC to 1 BC, the largest known piece of European Iron Age silverwork, found dismantled in a Danish peat bog in 1891.

sun-cross.name: Sun cross
sun-cross.summary: A prehistoric solar symbol of an equal-armed cross inside a circle, common in Neolithic to Bronze Age Europe, including many rock carvings across Scandinavia.

thrace.name: Thrace
thrace.summary: A historical and geographical region in Southeast Europe, roughly matching the Roman province of Thrace, spanning parts of modern Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey.

cimbri.name: Cimbri
cimbri.summary: An ancient tribe from Jutland who, with the Teutones, fought the Roman Republic between 113 and 101 BC, initially winning major victories before being crushed at the Battle of Vercellae.

teutons.name: Teutons
teutons.summary: An ancient northern European tribe, known chiefly for fighting Rome alongside the Cimbri in the Cimbrian War of the late 2nd century BC; their origins and language remain debated.

cimbrian-war.name: Cimbrian War
cimbrian-war.summary: A war (113–101 BC) between the Roman Republic and Germanic and Celtic tribes migrating from Jutland, inflicting Rome's heaviest losses since the Second Punic War before ending in Roman victory.

nydam-mose.name: Nydam Mose
nydam-mose.summary: An archaeological bog site in Denmark, near Sønderborg, where ancient artifacts have been preserved.

bracteate.name: Bracteate
bracteate.summary: A thin, single-sided gold medal worn as jewelry, mainly produced in Northern Europe during the Migration Period, also used for similar coins and clothing ornaments elsewhere.

pytheas.name: Pytheas
pytheas.summary: Greek geographer and explorer from Massalia (born c. 350 BC) who sailed to Northern Europe around 325 BC, circumnavigating Britain and becoming the first to describe the Arctic and the midnight sun.

pliny-the-elder.name: Pliny the Elder
pliny-the-elder.summary: A Roman author, naturalist and military commander (23/24–79 AD) who wrote the 37-volume encyclopedia Natural History and died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius.

natural-history-pliny.name: Natural History
natural-history-pliny.summary: Encyclopedic Latin work by Pliny the Elder, published around AD 77, the largest surviving single work from the Roman Empire, covering topics from astronomy to art and precious stones.

scania.name: Scania
scania.summary: Southernmost historical province of Sweden, roughly matching modern Skåne County; part of Denmark until ceded to Sweden by the 1658 Treaty of Roskilde.

silius-italicus.name: Silius Italicus
silius-italicus.summary: Roman senator and poet, c. 26–101 AD, who wrote the Punica, a 17-book epic on the Second Punic War and the longest surviving poem in Classical Latin.

picts.name: Picts
picts.summary: A group of peoples living in what is now Scotland north of the Firth of Forth during the Early Middle Ages, whose name may derive from the Latin word for 'painted'.

saaremaa.name: Saaremaa
saaremaa.summary: The largest island in Estonia, in the Baltic Sea, known by the name Ösel in most of the world from the 13th century until the 20th century.

gaius-julius-solinus.name: Solinus
gaius-julius-solinus.summary: Latin grammarian, geographer and compiler who probably flourished in the early to mid 3rd century AD.

tacitus.name: Tacitus
tacitus.summary: A Roman historian and politician (c. 56–120 AD) whose works Annals and Histories chronicled the empire, regarded as one of Rome's greatest historians.

nerthus.name: Nerthus
nerthus.summary: A goddess in Germanic paganism linked to a ceremonial wagon procession, described by the Roman historian Tacitus, and an early precursor to the Norse god Njörðr.

germania-book.name: Germania (book)
germania-book.summary: A work by the Roman historian Tacitus, written around 98 AD, describing the origins and customs of the Germanic peoples living outside the Roman Empire.

nj-r-r.name: Njörðr
nj-r-r.summary: A Norse god associated with the sea, navigation, fishing, wind and crop fertility, father of Freyr and Freyja and a member of the Vanir.

vanir.name: Vanir
vanir.summary: One of two main groups of Norse gods, associated with fertility, wisdom and foresight, alongside the other group, the Æsir.

jastorf-culture.name: Jastorf Culture
jastorf-culture.summary: An Iron Age material culture spanning parts of Germany, Jutland and Poland from the 6th to 1st centuries BC, forming the southern part of the Pre-Roman Iron Age.

hallstatt-culture.name: Hallstatt culture
hallstatt-culture.summary: A Western and Central European archaeological culture spanning the Late Bronze Age through Early Iron Age (12th-6th centuries BC), commonly linked to Proto-Celtic peoples.

la-t-ne-culture.name: La Tène culture
la-t-ne-culture.summary: A European Iron Age culture that flourished from about 450 BC until the Roman conquest, spanning France, Central Europe and beyond, known for its swirling decorative metalwork style.

yngling.name: Yngling dynasty
yngling.summary: Dynasty of kings first in Sweden and later Norway, known mainly through the poem Ynglingatal, claiming descent from the gods Freyr and Njörðr.

gamla-uppsala.name: Gamla Uppsala
gamla-uppsala.summary: A village near Uppsala, Sweden, that was a major religious and political center from the 3rd century CE, seat of the legendary Yngling kings and site of the assembly of all Swedes.

germania.name: Germania
germania.summary: A historical region of north-central Europe in Roman times, stretching roughly from the Rhine to the Vistula, associated by Roman writers with the Germanic peoples.

jordanes.name: Jordanes
jordanes.summary: 6th-century Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent turned historian, whose Getica is one of only two surviving ancient works on early Gothic history.

heruli.name: Heruli
heruli.summary: A smaller Germanic people of Late Antiquity who founded a kingdom near the Middle Danube after Attila's empire fell, later scattering to Scandinavia and the Balkans after conquest by the Lombards.

geats.name: Geats
geats.summary: A North Germanic tribe who inhabited Götaland in southern Sweden from antiquity to the late Middle Ages, ancestors of modern Swedes.

gutes.name: Gutes
gutes.summary: A North Germanic tribe that lived on the island of Gotland, related to the Goths and one of the ancestor groups of modern Swedes.

rugii.name: Rugii
rugii.summary: A small Germanic people first recorded near the Baltic in the 1st century who later formed a short-lived 5th-century kingdom on the Danube before being absorbed into the Ostrogothic Kingdom.

jutes.name: Jutes
jutes.summary: Germanic people who settled in Britain after the Romans left; according to Bede, one of the three most powerful Germanic nations, ancestors of the people of Kent and the Isle of Wight.

angles-tribe.name: Angles
angles-tribe.summary: One of the main Germanic peoples who settled in Britain after the Roman period, founding several kingdoms and giving their name to England and the English language.

snorri-sturluson.name: Snorri Sturluson
snorri-sturluson.summary: An Icelandic historian, poet and politician (1179–1241) credited with the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, key sources on Norse mythology and kings; he was assassinated in 1241.

heimskringla.name: Heimskringla
heimskringla.summary: The best-known collection of Old Norwegian kings' sagas, written in Old Norse in Iceland and likely composed by Snorri Sturluson around 1230.

poetic-edda.name: Poetic Edda
poetic-edda.summary: A collection of anonymous Old Norse poems in alliterative verse, based on the medieval Icelandic Codex Regius manuscript, central to the study of Norse mythology.

h-vam-l.name: Hávamál
h-vam-l.summary: Old Norse poem attributed to Odin, dated to around 900–1000 CE, offering practical and philosophical wisdom on conduct, plus an account of how Odin won the runes.

odin.name: Odin
odin.summary: A widely revered god of Norse mythology and Germanic paganism, associated with wisdom, poetry and frenzy, worshipped from Roman-era Germania through the Viking Age.

nicomachean-ethics.name: Nicomachean Ethics
nicomachean-ethics.summary: Aristotle's best-known work on ethics, exploring how to live well and what constitutes the good; hugely influential on medieval philosophy.

elder-futhark.name: Elder Futhark
elder-futhark.summary: The oldest form of the runic alphabets, used by Germanic peoples from the 2nd to 8th centuries; its reading was forgotten until deciphered in 1865.

gu-mundur-finnbogason.name: Guðmundur Finnbogason
gu-mundur-finnbogason.summary: Icelandic philosopher (1873–1944) and one of the first Icelandic psychologists, whose work influenced Jean Piaget's development stages model.

sveinbjorn-johnson.name: Sveinbjorn Johnson
sveinbjorn-johnson.summary: Icelandic-born American lawyer, politician and scholar (1883-1946).

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Ancient Greek poet, possibly born around the 8th century BC, traditionally credited as author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, foundational works of Greek literature.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

berserker.name: berserkir
berserker.summary: Scandinavian warriors described in Old Norse sources as fighting in a trance-like fury, the origin of the modern English word "berserk."

gudme.name: Gudme
gudme.summary: A town in southern Denmark on the island of Funen, formerly seat of the now-merged Gudme municipality.

helg.name: Helgö
helg.summary: A small island in Lake Mälaren, Sweden, about 5 km long.

lee-m-hollander.name: Lee M. Hollander
lee-m-hollander.summary: An American philologist (1880–1972) who specialized in Old Norse studies and led the Germanic Languages department at the University of Texas at Austin.

vedas.name: Vedas
vedas.summary: A large body of ancient Indian religious texts and the oldest layer of Sanskrit literature, orally transmitted since the 2nd millennium BCE and regarded as the oldest scriptures of Hinduism.

upp-kra.name: Uppåkra
upp-kra.summary: A village in Scania, southern Sweden, known for an Iron Age archaeological site excavated since 1996.

rock-carvings-in-tanum.name: Tanumshede
rock-carvings-in-tanum.summary: Site near this Swedish town in Bohuslän holding a dense collection of rock carvings, declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.

rock-carvings-at-alta.name: Alta
rock-carvings-at-alta.summary: Municipality in northern Norway with over 6,000 rock carvings dated from about 4200 to 500 BCE, showing a hunter-gatherer culture skilled in reindeer herding and boat building.

bohusl-n.name: Bohuslän
bohusl-n.summary: A Swedish coastal province bordering Norway, held as a Norwegian territory from the 870s until ceded to Sweden by the 1658 Treaty of Roskilde.
